one_liner: Multithreaded C++ Redis 6.2 fork serving one keyspace from many event-loop threads; claims ~7x Redis 6 throughput under TLS.
what_it_does: KeyDB is a Redis server fork (feature parity with Redis 6.2.3 as of v6.2.0) that speaks the Redis protocol and is meant to accept Redis clients, modules, Lua scripts and redis.conf files unchanged, so the switch is a binary swap. On top of Redis it adds multithreaded request serving (server-threads), active-active replication (active-replica, multi-master), per-member expiry (EXPIREMEMBER), non-blocking KEYS/SCAN, S3 backup/restore and an experimental RocksDB-backed FLASH tier.
how_it_is_fast: It runs the stock Redis ae event loop on N threads and pins each connection to one thread at accept() (spread with Linux SO_REUSEPORT plus active client balancing), so socket I/O, TLS and RESP parsing run in parallel. Command execution against the shared keyspace is still serialized by a single global lock: a fair ticket spinlock ('fastlock', with an x86-64 assembly fast path) that spins with pause/yield and falls back to a futex wait, and that uses otherwise wasted spin time to do incremental dict rehashing ('async rehash'). KEYS/SCAN, and optionally GET/MGET ('enable-async-commands') and in-process BGSAVE ('use-fork no'), read from copy-on-write MVCC snapshots of the database so they do not hold the global lock.
when_to_use: A single Redis 6.x node that is CPU-bound on networking, TLS or protocol parsing (many connections, small GET/SET values) and you want more ops/s from one box without sharding into Redis Cluster or running one instance per core
TLS-terminated Redis traffic: the benchmarked Redis 6 could not combine io-threads with TLS, while KeyDB does TLS on every server thread
Existing Redis 6.x deployments on Linux (Redis 6 RDB files, modules, Lua) that want a binary swap and can tolerate a stale codebase
You specifically need active-active (multi-master) replication or per-member hash/set expiry, which upstream Redis does not provide
when_not_to_use: New production deployments: no commits since April 2024, last release v6.3.4 (Oct 2023), the lead developer left Snap in early 2025 and told users to move to Valkey, and deadlock/crash issues (e.g. #883 replication deadlock, #743, #827) remain open
Anything needing Redis 7+ commands or data: RDB_VERSION is 9, so Redis 7 dumps (RDB v10) fail to load (#527) and Redis 7 commands such as PEXPIRETIME are missing
Write-heavy or hot-key workloads and long MULTI/EXEC or Lua: every command still runs under one global lock (transactions hold it for the whole EXEC), so parallelism is limited to I/O and parsing
Non-Linux hosts, and ARM with caution: the threading model relies on Linux SO_REUSEPORT load balancing, and there are open ARM startup-assert reports (#856)

Multi-master or FLASH setups you cannot babysit: FLASH is labelled experimental/beta, active replication has an open data-consistency report (#366), and HN users reported cluster-wide crashes and deadlocks in multi-master mode

integration.form: standalone server binary (keydb-server, built with make; Docker image eqalpha/keydb); not a linkable library
integration.dependencies: Bundled in deps/: jemalloc, Lua, hiredis, linenoise, hdr_histogram, moodycamel concurrentqueue, cpp-statsd-client, memkind (optional), RocksDB submodule (FLASH only). System: OpenSSL (TLS on by default), libuuid, libcurl (MOTD, disable with NO_MOTD=yes), nasm (x86-64 spinlock), bz2/zstd/lz4/snappy for RocksDB builds; Makefile can link system jemalloc/RocksDB/hiredis instead
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (-std=c++17 -fno-rtti) plus C11/C99 for the C files; GCC or Clang (Clang builds use libc++); GCC 13.1 build fixed in 6.3.4; minimum compiler versions not documented
integration.platforms: Linux (tested); x86-64 gets the assembly spinlock, aarch64 builds exist but have open crash reports; FreeBSD compiles as of 6.3.4; macOS builds but README says only Linux is supported for the threading model
integration.thread_safety: Server process, so clients get Redis semantics; internally a global keyspace spinlock, EXEC holds it for the whole transaction, and modules run under a GIL taken only when all server threads are paused. With enable-async-commands, writes from other clients may become visible after a delay (max-snapshot-slip); use LFENCE if you need cross-client ordering
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — protocol, modules, scripts and config compatible with Redis 6.2 (io-threads is aliased to server-threads), but no Redis 7+ commands or RDB v10 and the multithreading is Linux-only

gotchas: server-threads should follow NIC queue count, not core count: the README recommends 4 (default 2) and warns more threads can be slower because the global lock is a spinlock, yet the headline TLS benchmark used 16 threads with affinity
An existing redis.conf with 'io-threads 8' silently becomes 8 KeyDB server threads, since io-threads is an alias for server-threads
KeyDB expects exclusive use of its cores (spinning waiters burn CPU), and keydb-benchmark/redis-benchmark are single-threaded and too slow to measure it; use memtier on separate cores
multi-master-no-forward yes loses data unless every master is in a full mesh; enable-async-commands relaxes cross-client read-your-writes ordering and currently covers only GET/MGET
verified_claims_summary: KeyDB's own blog (Sept 2020) drove servers on an AWS m5.4xlarge from an m5.8xlarge with memtier_benchmark --tls --threads=32 and otherwise default settings: KeyDB with 16 server threads and TLS got close to 1M ops/s (about 800k with 8 threads) versus ~130k ops/s for single-threaded Redis 6.0 with TLS, which is 36% below non-TLS single-threaded Redis and 61% below non-TLS Redis with io-threads. CPU model, compiler, build flags and exact versions are not given, Redis was not sharded or run as several instances, and the 'up to 7x lower latency' claim has no table.
status_note: Stale: last release v6.3.4 (Oct 2023) and last commit April 2024, and the lead developer, leaving Snap, recommended Valkey. The code is BSD-3-Clause and builds with make, but anyone adopting it maintains the fork themselves.
